summary: Reports measurements of FTP user and server programs taken over about six months. It covers the measurement criteria and tools, the results, how they compare with other data, and asks readers for suggestions on the measurement and summary methods.

plainLanguage.summary: Someone timed how fast files moved over the network for half a year and shares the results, asking others whether he measured the right way.

questions: how fast was early arpanet file transfer
subtitle: Measurements of file transfer speeds and reliability over the ARPANET.

tldr.problem: FTP was becoming widely used on the ARPANET, but there were no published measurements of its actual performance and reliability characteristics.
tldr.mechanism: MIT-DMS built automated measurement facilities to track transfer rate, response time, availability, and processing cost. They monitored FTP transfers from February to August 1973, recording data on 304 file transfers.
tldr.outcome: The measurements showed FTP worked reliably with an average transfer rate of 7.56 kilobits per second, and that 36-bit transfers were about five times faster than 8-bit ASCII transfers.

today: RFC 573 is a historical report on early FTP performance. It is not a specification or standard, but is valuable for understanding the capabilities and limitations of the original ARPANET.

sections.title: Why Measure FTP
sections.content: As FTP use grew on the ARPANET, the MIT-DMS team wanted to understand how well it actually performed. They identified six key measurement categories: transfer rate (throughput), response time (delay), processing cost (CPU and dollars), failure-to-connect rate, availability (percentage uptime), and accuracy (error rate). The goal was to gather real data to help ARPANET users and programmers make decisions about network usage and optimization.
sections.plainLanguage: People wanted to know if file transfer was fast, reliable, and cheap to use.

sections.title: How They Measured
sections.content: The MIT-DMS CALICO subsystem automatically recorded detailed data every time its FTP client or server transferred files. For each transfer, it logged the remote host, date, time, total bits, real-time elapsed, CPU time used, whether it was sending or receiving, and the FTP settings used (byte size, representation type, transfer mode, file structure). The resulting data was displayed and summarized by specialized programs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each file transfer was automatically logged like a receipt, recording how long it took and how much computer work it required.

sections.title: The Results
sections.content: Over six months (February to August 1973), 304 files totaling 57.6 million bits were transferred. The average transfer rate was 7.56 kilobits per second. The most efficient mode was 36-bit Image transfer (used by PDP-10 systems), which achieved 9.35 kilobits per second and required only 3 CPU seconds per megabit. ASCII-8 transfer was much slower at 2.09 kilobits per second and consumed 19 CPU seconds per megabit. The fastest single transfer recorded was 27.8 kilobits per second, a retrieval from BBN-TENEXA.
sections.plainLanguage: Files moved at about 7.5 thousand bits per second on average, but 36-bit transfers were much faster and less work for the computer than 8-bit transfers.

sections.title: Implications and Recommendations
sections.content: The data showed the ARPANET and FTP were quite reliable: the team transferred complete operating system listings of 6 million bits, reassembled them, and ran the code without errors. The measurements also revealed that small files transferred slower than large ones, and that large network buffers and allocations improved performance significantly. The author recommended that protocol designers favor 36-bit Image transfer for PDP-10 systems and requested feedback from other ARPANET users on the measurement methodology itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The network worked well and was pretty reliable. Using bigger buffers and the right transfer mode made things faster.
